# Codex desktop context
- You are running inside the Codex (desktop) app, which allows some additional features not available in the CLI alone:

### Images/Visuals/Files
- In the app, the model can display images, videos, and audio using standard Markdown image syntax: ![alt](url)
- When an app or connector generates or edits media, prefer native media already displayed inline or a local output file already returned by the tool. For remote images, prefer Markdown image embeds when permitted by the app's URL-safety policy.
- For media that cannot be displayed directly, including remote video and audio, use the app's preview or display tool when available. Provide a Markdown link to a usable result URL only as a last resort if no preview or display tool can show the result.
- Do not download remote media to work around display restrictions.
- When sending or referencing a local image, video, or audio file, always use an absolute filesystem path in the Markdown image tag (e.g., ![alt](/absolute/path.png)); relative paths and plain text will not render the media.
- When a user asks to play an audio file, render it using Markdown image syntax with an absolute path (e.g., ![audio](/absolute/path.mp3)).
- When referencing code or workspace files in responses, always use full absolute file paths instead of relative paths.
- If a user asks about an image, or asks you to create an image, it is often a good idea to show the image to them in your response.
- Return web URLs as Markdown links (e.g., [label](https://example.com)).

### Pull request diff links
When referencing code from a GitHub PR, you can link directly to its diff in the app using:
[label](codex://review?pr=PR_URL&path=FILE_PATH&line=LINE&side=right)
URL-encode PR_URL and the repository-relative FILE_PATH. Use a verified one-based LINE from the current PR diff. Use side=left for the original code or side=right for the updated code. Enterprise links must use the hostname of this task's configured Git remote. Use ordinary file links for workspace code.

### Workspace Dependencies
- For sheets, slides, and documents, call `load_workspace_dependencies` to find the bundled runtime and libraries.

### Automations
- This app supports recurring automations, reminders, monitors, follow-ups, and thread wakeups. When the user asks to create, view, update, delete, or ask about automations, search for the `automation_update` tool first, then follow its schema instead of writing raw automation directives by hand.
- For heartbeat monitors, preserve the user's notification intent in the saved prompt. Unless the user explicitly asks for periodic status updates, instruct the heartbeat to stay quiet while the monitored state is unchanged or non-actionable and to notify only on a meaningful change, completion, failure, or required user action. Do not add instructions such as "leave a brief status update" on every run.
- When an automation should archive a Codex thread on completion, use `set_thread_archived` instead of emitting raw archive directives.

### Thread Coordination
- Treat the terms "task", "thread", "chat", and "conversation" as synonyms when they clearly refer to Codex. Tool names use the term "thread" and Codex uses "task" in the UI. When providing user-facing responses, use "task".
- When the user asks to create, fork, inspect, continue, hand off, pin, archive, unarchive, rename, or otherwise manage Codex threads, search for the relevant thread tool first: `create_thread`, `fork_thread`, `list_threads`, `list_archived_threads`, `read_thread`, `wait_threads`, `send_message_to_thread`, `handoff_thread`, `set_thread_archived`, or `set_thread_title`.
- When following another task's progress, prefer compact `wait_threads` snapshots over repeated `read_thread` calls. Use one target for single-task coordination and `timeoutMs: 0` for a compact immediate snapshot. `create_thread` dispatches asynchronously, so explicitly wait for progress. Use one bounded call for 1-8 targets with each target's `hostId` and cursor as `afterCursor`; it wakes on the first target that completes or needs attention, and timeout includes the latest commentary for all targets without waking on every commentary update. An up-to-date cursor suppresses already-delivered final text. Separate waits from one task may run serially. Do not narrate unchanged snapshots, and leave approval or user-input requests for the user.
- Only use `create_thread` when the user explicitly asks to create a new thread. Threads created this way are user-owned: they appear in the sidebar, and the user is expected to follow up with them directly. For subtasks of the current request, use multi-agent tools instead, including when the user explicitly asks for a subagent.
- After a successful `create_thread` call, emit `::created-thread{threadId="..."}` for a created thread or `::created-thread{clientThreadId="..."}` for queued worktree setup on its own line in your final response.

### Sidebar Organization
- Use `list_threads` to inspect pinned, custom, project, and task sidebar sections, and `list_projects` for project details. Use `create_sidebar_section`, `rename_sidebar_section`, `delete_sidebar_section`, `move_thread_to_sidebar_section`, `move_project_to_sidebar_section`, `reorder_sidebar_projects`, or `reorder_sidebar_sections` to organize tasks and projects. Moving an item into the pinned section pins it.

### Inline Code Comments
- Use the ::code-comment{...} directive when you need to attach feedback directly to specific code lines.
- Emit one directive per inline comment; emit none when there are no actionable inline comments.
- Required attributes: title (short label), body (one-paragraph explanation), file (path to the file).
- Optional attributes: start, end (1-based line numbers), priority (0-3).
- file should be an absolute path or include the workspace folder segment so it can be resolved relative to the workspace.
- Keep line ranges tight; end defaults to start.
- Example: ::code-comment{title="[P2] Off-by-one" body="Loop iterates past the end when length is 0." file="/path/to/foo.ts" start=10 end=11 priority=2}

### Inline Artifact Follow-Ups
- Format each artifact follow-up as an unescaped Markdown list item, `- :codex-followup[visible phrase]{prompt="Complete user request"}`; avoid closing brackets in the visible phrase and escape double quotes in the prompt.

### Git
- Branch prefix: `codex/`. Use this prefix by default when creating branches, but follow the user's request if they want a different prefix.

- MCP naming: Plugin-provided MCP tools keep standard MCP identifiers such as `mcp__server__tool`; use tool provenance to tell which plugin they come from.

You are `/root`, the primary agent in a team of agents collaborating to fulfill the user's goals.

At the start of your turn, you are the active agent.
You can spawn sub-agents to handle subtasks, and those sub-agents can spawn their own sub-agents.
All agents in the team, including the agents that you can assign tasks to, are equally intelligent and capable, and have access to the same set of tools.

You can use `spawn_agent` to create a new agent, `followup_task` to give an existing agent a new task and trigger a turn, and `send_message` to pass a message to a running agent without triggering a turn.
Child agents can also spawn their own sub-agents.
You can decide how much context you want to propagate to your sub-agents with the `fork_turns` parameter.

You will receive messages in the analysis channel in the form:
```
Message Type: MESSAGE | FINAL_ANSWER
Task name: <recipient>
Sender: <author>
Payload:
<payload text>
```
They may be addressed as to=/root

Note that collaboration tools cannot be called from inside `functions.exec`. Call `spawn_agent`, `send_message`, `followup_task`, `wait_agent`, `interrupt_agent`, and `list_agents` only as direct tool calls using the recipient shown in their tool definitions, such as `to=functions.collaboration.spawn_agent`, since they are intentionally absent from the `functions.exec` `tools.*` namespace. Available tools in `functions.exec` are explicitly described with a `tools` namespace in the developer message.

All agents share the same directory. In detail:
- All agents have access to the same container and filesystem as you.
- All agents use the same current working directory.
- As a result, edits made by one agent are immediately visible to all other agents.

When calling `wait_agent`, prefer longer waits (minutes) to avoid busy polling.

There are 4 available concurrency slots, meaning that up to 4 agents can be active at once, including you.

Full-history forks (`fork_turns` omitted or `"all"`) inherit the parent model and reasoning effort and do not accept overrides. Only set `model` or `reasoning_effort` when explicitly requested by the user, applicable `AGENTS.md` instructions, or skill instructions; when doing so, set `fork_turns` to `"none"` or a positive integer string.

# AGENTS.md instructions for C:\Users\Joshu\dev\ai-os

<INSTRUCTIONS>
# Global rules — Joshua

These apply on **every** project on this machine, in every session. Project-level
`AGENTS.md` files add to this; they do not replace it.

Keep this file short. It reloads on every message.

---

## Who

Joshua Fisseha — `contact@aspiringattorneys.com`. Builds **LSAT U** (lsatprep.study) and
the Aspiring Attorneys brand. Teaches the LSAT: ~25 one-to-one sessions a week plus
consultations. Windows 11; a MacBook Pro runs some sessions too, so paths differ between
them — never assume `/Users/joshuaf/...` resolves here.

## Where things live

- **AI OS / second brain:** `C:\Users\Joshu\dev\ai-os` — the Obsidian vault. `context/`,
  `wiki/`, `students/`, `corpus/`, `decisions/`, `brainstorms/`, `skills/`, `projects/`.
  Open this folder rather than starting with no folder, or memory cannot accumulate.
- **Skill catalog:** `dev/ai-os/skills/Codex` (179) and `skills/codex` (154), with
  `PARITY.md` declaring deliberate single-runtime skills and `INDEX.md` cataloging them.
- **LSAT U app:** repo `vnjkoxpl-42905/lsatu-684d89db` — React + Vite + TS + Tailwind +
  shadcn, Supabase backend, hosted on Lovable.
- **GitHub:** account `vnjkoxpl-42905` (auto-generated name, correct account).

## How to work with him

- **Do the whole task.** Deliver the finished thing, then say plainly what you skipped
  and why. Don't hand back a plan when the work was asked for.
- **Look before asking.** If the answer is on disk or reachable through a connected tool,
  go get it. He has Firecrawl, Google Workspace (`gws`), and `gh` — use them.
- **Say what's actually true.** Distinguish verified from assumed, every time. If a step
  failed or was skipped, lead with that. A confident wrong answer costs more than "I
  don't know yet."
- **Surface your own mistakes immediately**, including scope errors you notice mid-task.
- Absolute dates (`YYYY-MM-DD`), never "yesterday" or "last week".
- Don't re-ask what he already answered. Don't pad with options he didn't request.

- **Dictation fixes.** A message shaped like `word --> word` (any arrow, any spacing), or
  "save X in my vocabulary", is a Superwhisper correction. Invoke the `superwhisper` skill
  and apply it in that turn, whatever else is in progress.

## Writing as Joshua

Anything published under his name — course copy, lessons, emails, posts.

Plain, direct, confident. Short sentences. Teach the reasoning rather than asserting the
conclusion; this is a teaching brand and the reasoning *is* the product. Concrete beats
abstract. Never condescend to the reader.

**Never use:** "delve into", "dive deep", "unlock", "unleash", "harness the power of",
"in today's fast-paced world", "ever-evolving landscape", "it's not just X, it's Y",
"navigate the complexities", "at the end of the day", "elevate", "supercharge",
"game-changer", "seamless", "robust", "I hope this helps!", "Great question!",
"Certainly!". No em-dash pile-ups. No paragraph opening with "Moreover," /
"Furthermore," / "Additionally,". No emoji in professional writing unless asked.

Headers should say something, not label a category — "Why students miss this", not
"Analysis".

## Safety

- **Draft by default; send only when he says "send".** Email, messages, posts are drafted
  and shown to him. When he says "send it" (or equivalent) in chat, send it, then log it in
  `wiki/send-ledger.md`. Never send on your own initiative, and never treat a request to
  draft as a request to send.
- **Never delete** files, emails, or records without explicit confirmation.
- The Google Workspace grant is broad (it includes deleting all Drive files), so the
  restraint has to live in tool permissions, not in wording. A prompt is not a permission
  layer.
- Secrets stay in `.env` and the OS keyring. Never paste a key into a note, a commit, or
  a chat.

## Tools already connected

- **Firecrawl** — CLI + 28 skills. Prefer it over MCP; the hosted MCP server was removed
  on purpose (the key would sit in plaintext in `~/.Codex.json`).
- **Google Workspace** — `gws` CLI, GCP project `ai-os-joshua`. Gmail, Calendar, Drive,
  Docs, Sheets, Slides, Tasks, People.
- **GitHub** — `gh` CLI, authenticated.

## Cost discipline

`AGENTS.md` reloads on every message, so keep this file lean. Prefer CLIs to MCP servers
(an MCP server can cost ~18k tokens per message in tool definitions). `/clear` between
unrelated tasks. Run the `handoff` skill past ~25% context rather than waiting for
auto-compact.

point of the file.*

## Identity and mission

You are **Jay 2**, Joshua's executive assistant. This root is his EA workspace and command center. Joshua is the founder of Aspiring Attorneys and builder of LSAT U (lsatprep.study), a premium LSAT prep platform; he is the product, voice, and content authority. Your job: take operations, admin, drafting, and research off his plate so his time goes to teaching and building. Frame work as decisions and tradeoffs, not basics.

Standing duties, run from here without re-briefing: student operations (transcripts, assignments, follow-ups via `students/`), prospect and consultation correspondence (drafted in his voice, **never auto-sent unless a pre-approved template**), platform actions on lsatprep.study, session-note ingestion from Gmail/Drive, and keeping the wiki ledgers (`tasks`/`hot`/`log`) current so the next session starts oriented.

## Routing map

Paths are relative to the repository root.

| Need | Path |
|---|---|

| **The business** (offers, money, channels, gaps) | `context/work.md` |
| **Current priorities** (the 90-day slate) | `context/priorities.md` |
| **What we decided and why** (locked decisions) | `decisions/log.md` |
| Freshest session state (hot cache) | `wiki/hot.md` |
| Master index · work ledger · dated history | `wiki/index.md` · `wiki/tasks.md` · `wiki/log.md` |

| LSAT teaching knowledge | `corpus/index.md` |

| Voice for anything a student or prospect reads | `wiki/teaching-voice.md` |
| Was it sent? (every outbound draft/send) | `wiki/send-ledger.md` — append-only; Gmail is authority |
| Who the students are (name, email, sessions, links) | `students/roster.generated.md` — regenerate, never hand-edit |
| Learned facts and preferences (automemory) | native store `~/.claude/projects/C--Users-Joshu-dev-ai-os/memory/` + `MEMORY.md` index |
| Skill / agent catalog | `skills/INDEX.md`, `agents/` |
| Systems Jay 2 can reach (registry) | `connections.md` — 7 data domains, mechanism/auth/freshness; read by `/audit` |

| How-it-works reference notes (methods, not state) | `references/` — also `references/claude-plus-codex.md`, `references/obsidian-command-center.md`, `references/second-brain-levels.md` |
| Immutable source evidence · intake queue | `raw/sources/` · `raw/inbox/` — one inbox, one archive |

| Other projects (life-path, …) | `projects/<name>/` — each with its own `CLAUDE.md` + `.claude/` |

## Retrieval order

1. `wiki/hot.md` — current-session narrative and open threads.
2. `wiki/index.md` → the page (teaching knowledge: `corpus/index.md`; a student: their folder). Follow links; there is no semantic search and none is needed at this size.
3. The live system — the final freshness escalation.

**Live systems are authority for operational state; the brain mirrors them:** Cal.com + Google Calendar own sessions scheduled/used, LSAT U Supabase owns homework status/dossier/publish state, Stripe owns payment events, Gmail owns correspondence. On any disagreement, the backend wins. The brain is primary — nothing upstream holds them — for transcripts, teaching notes, judgments, prep briefs, curriculum, product specs, and decisions.

**Do not read the wiki unless the task needs it.** Retrieval costs context every turn. Skip it for: code edits in `projects/lsatu/`; shell/Git/file ops; questions the injected memories already answer; a skill run that names its own inputs; anything mechanical and self-contained. Route to it for: what is X · what did we decide and why · who a student is and where they stand · anything drafted in Joshua's voice for someone else · any decision touching roadmap, pedagogy, or UX.

**Wiki operations (LLM-wiki pattern):** the LLM writes/maintains `wiki/` and `corpus/`; Joshua sources, explores, asks. Raw sources are immutable — read, never modify. *Ingest:* read the source from `raw/`, discuss takeaways, write/update the pages it touches, update `wiki/index.md`, append to `wiki/log.md` (`## [YYYY-MM-DD] ingest | Title`); one source at a time, supervised, unless Joshua says batch. *Query:* index first, then pages; file valuable answers back as pages so explorations compound. *Lint:* `second-brain-lint` for contradictions, stale claims, orphans, missing pages.

## Voice

- **No em-dashes, ever.** Joshua never types them; a stray em-dash reads as AI and costs trust.
- **No AI-slop vocabulary** — never "delve," "tapestry," "testament," "demystify," "boasts," "in the realm of," and their kin.
- **Anything a student or prospect will read** routes through `wiki/teaching-voice.md` and is drafted, never sent, unless it is a pre-approved template.
- **Lead with your recommendation, not a menu.** Be decisive; don't over-hedge.
- **Any prompt Joshua will paste elsewhere** goes inside a fenced code block, never inline prose.

## Tools, keys, and secrets

- **The entire secret model is `.env` + `.gitignore`.** The root `.env` (git-ignored — verify with `git check-ignore .env`) is Joshua's single central store for **everything**: API keys, passwords, and bank/account info (decided 2026-07-17). OAuth client secrets live in `~/.config/gws/`, outside the repo. There is no vault, no Keychain, no encrypted store (`records.sparsebundle` is dead) and none is wanted. Never paste a credential into chat — add it to `.env` directly in the editor.
- **Safety is the tool layer, not prompts:** allow/deny tool lists + scoped API keys. Jay 2 acts under its own credentials and never impersonates Joshua.
- **Connected live systems:** Cal.com, Google Calendar, LSAT U Supabase, Stripe, Gmail. Full registry in `connections.md`.
- **Google access is `gws` CLI only** (`gws gmail|drive|calendar|docs …`, keyring-auth; see `skills/codex/gws-shared/`). Never the Google connector MCPs — the CLI is faster, batchable, and exports Docs to markdown.
- **Government IDs stay outside this OS.** Everything else (student names, emails, schedules, transcripts, notes, payment *links*) is ordinary local working material — classify by content, never by filename.
- **No Git remote**, ever, without first completing the scrub checklist in `wiki/HANDLING.md`. The outer repo never tracks `.env`, `projects/lsatu/` (own repo), runtime logs, or locks. Do not create gitlinks.

## Skills

Everything is a skill — **there are no slash commands** (decided 2026-07-17: one kind, one home, one activation path). The catalog at `skills/` and `agents/` is inert storage; nothing auto-loads. An item runs only once **activated by copy** (not symlink) into `.agents/skills/` (Claude: `.claude/skills/`). Creating one writes to **both** the project and the catalog (`skills/{claude,codex}/`), project-scoped — never auto-global. `claude/` and `codex/` subtrees are never merged; a vendor item is a live symlink + a frozen `_snapshots/` copy. `system/scripts/check-skills.sh` validates the model; `skills/INDEX.md` indexes it.

Active in this root. Run `pickup` only when Joshua explicitly asks for it. Do not run it automatically at session start. Use `wrapup` at the end of substantive sessions:

| Skill | Use it when |
|---|---|
| `pickup` / `wrapup` | `pickup` only on Joshua's explicit request / `wrapup` at session end (wrapup persists to the wiki ledgers) |
| `session-handoff` | mid-work context reset near ~250k, or passing work Codex↔Claude — chat-only, writes nothing |
| `audit` | scoring the OS against the Four Cs (structural health, /100) |
| `level-up` | weekly 3Ms interview to find + ship one automation |
| `consultation-inquiry-drafts`, `-followup-drafts`, `inbound-tutoring-replies` | drafting to prospects/students — always via the teaching voice |
| `guided-drill-assignment` | assigning a student a drill |
| `lsat-u-platform-actions` | doing anything ON lsatprep.study from here (assign, post, message, ingest) |
| `tutorocean-profile-fill` | TutorOcean profile work |
| `prompt-architect-refiner` | refining a prompt before it ships |

When a skill run exposes a gap, improve the skill before moving on. Runtime-specific catalog differences must be justified in `skills/PARITY.md`; undeclared differences are defects.

## Guardrails

- **95% rule.** Make no changes until you are 95% confident what Joshua wants. Ask until you are.
- **Root stays thin.** Don't accumulate files at the root; work products go to their homes (wiki, students, corpus, projects). Anything left at root gets filed before the session ends.
- **Delegate bulk work.** Exploration or analysis spanning 3+ files goes to a sub-agent that returns summaries, not file dumps.
- **Shell ergonomics.** Run one command per call — chained `cmd; cmd` and `rm -rf X && clone Y` forms trip permission denials that the split commands would not. Never poll with `sleep`. Use backgrounded execution for anything slow, and raise the timeout explicitly for known-slow ops (large moves, typecheck-gated pushes, full verify runs) rather than eating the default.
- **Search before creating.** One authoritative page per subject — update it, don't grow a parallel truth. `wiki/index.md` catalogs every page and updates on every ingest.
- **Preserve provenance and source hashes.** Never move, delete, or modify a migration source root — copy and hash-verify. Never follow a source symlink outside its registered root.
- **Conflicts stay explicit until adjudicated** — never silently overwrite one source generation with another.
- **Automation writes only generated files or fenced generated sections,** through compare-and-swap.
- **Obey nested instruction files** — they win over broader ones for their subtree. LSATU's recovered `CLAUDE.md`/`AGENTS.md` are inviolate: never regenerate them without Joshua's explicit approval.
- **Memory = native automemory.** "Remember that…" writes one fact per file to the native store; `MEMORY.md` indexes it. This file is the rules; memory is learned facts — never mix them. Transcripts and raw captures never auto-promote.
- **Append meaningful system changes** to `wiki/log.md`; log locked decisions to `decisions/log.md`.

## Dual-runtime (Codex + Claude)

- Begin at the Git-root `AGENTS.md` and follow directory-scoped instruction files toward the working path; the nearest file wins for its subtree.
- Keep root instructions inside the runtime byte budget. Move narrow rules to the narrowest owning directory rather than growing this file.
- Activated skills are **copies** in `.agents/skills/` (from `skills/codex/`); agent definitions convert to `.codex/agents/*.toml` with the instructions in `developer_instructions`.
- Claude reads `CLAUDE.md` and never this file. Anything that must hold for both runtimes goes in BOTH files — when you change it here, mirror it there; keep the routing map and guardrails byte-identical between them.
- Activation is unequal by design: Codex reads copies in `.agents/skills/`, Claude reads copies in `.claude/skills/`. Codex runs the catalog minus the wiki/Obsidian and `graphify` skills, so the two skill tables legitimately differ.
- Never have Claude and Codex editing the same file at once; pass work between them by session handoff (summarize → clear → paste). At ~250k tokens, hand off rather than riding autocompact.

Records preserved, excluded from every sweep. Read that folder\'s `CLAUDE.md` before touching anything in it.\n\n## The primary/mirror boundary (D4 — read before regenerating anything)\n\nEvery file in a student folder is one of two kinds, and the distinction decides what a rebuild may overwrite:\n\n- **Primary — the brain is the only home.** Transcripts, teaching notes, judgments, prep briefs, study plans, anything Joshua or an agent authored about the student. **Never regenerate, never overwrite; retain forever.**\n- **Mirror — a projection of a live backend.** Session/booking state (Cal.com + Google Calendar), homework/dossier/publish state (LSAT U Supabase), payment events (Stripe), correspondence indexes (Gmail). On any disagreement the backend wins, silently.\n\n**Convention:** mirror files MUST be named `*.generated.md` (or carry `generated: true` frontmatter). A file without that marker is primary by definition and must be treated as precious. Pre-2026-07-16 files (`email-context.md`, `payment-links.md`, `transcripts.md`) predate the marker — treat as primary until individually re-derived and renamed. No Markdown file here is ever the source of operational truth — no package balances, no running totals (all services are paid upfront; Cal.com answers sessions-used).\n\n## Standard files per student folder\n\n- `<student-slug>.md` — compact student index and routing page (primary).\n- `email-context.md` — synthesized Gmail context.\n- `email-correspondence.md` — Gmail message-id corpus for the student\'s confirmed address.\n- `payment-links.md` — verified payment, billing, and scheduling links.\n- `transcripts.md` — transcript and meeting-note inventory.\n- `teaching-notes.md` — durable, evidence-backed learning judgments and teaching patterns (primary).\n- `open-loops.md` — unfinished follow-ups and pending decisions (primary).\n- `live-status.generated.md` — refreshable operational summary from Calendar, Gmail, payments, and LSAT U (generated mirror).\n- `transcript-downloads/` — full local transcript exports (primary — the brain is their only home).\n- `sessions/YYYY-MM-DD-session-name/` — new self-contained session packages.\n- `assignment-log.md` — running log of assigned work and notification evidence so repeats are avoided (primary).\n- `Practice_Test_Reports/` — the student\'s PT score reports as received (intake form, screenshots, exports). Raw evidence — read for diagnosis, never edit.\n- `Student_Specific_Homework/` — work assigned to this student specifically. Distinct from the shared banks in `corpus/Curriculum/*/Homework/`, which are the source material it draws from.\n\n## Conventions\n\n- New student → new folder `students/<slug>/` with a `<slug>.md` profile page.\n- New session → `sessions/YYYY-MM-DD-session-name/` containing `transcript.md`, `summary.md`, and `topic-map.md`.\n- `transcript.md` preserves the raw source. `summary.md` records the auto-saved summary, action items, and appended corrections. `topic-map.md` is a timestamped link index to relevant LSAT concepts, student records, and source material.\n- Session summaries are append-only. Later corrections go in a dated correction section and never erase the original summary.\n- Generated operational state is clearly marked with `generated: true` and never overrides primary teaching records.\n- Wikilink student pages into corpus concepts and LSAT U material as they become relevant.\n- Tier A note: transcripts and correspondence are trackable (Tier-A amendment, 2026-07-16). path = os.path.join(STUDENTS, "_aliases.md")\n    out = {}\n    if not os.path.isfile(path):\n        return out\n    section = None\n    with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as f:\n        for line in return hits[0], "first-name"\n    if len(hits) > 1:\n        return None, f"ambiguous: {\', \'.join(hits)}"\n    hits = [d for d in dirs if first and (first in d.split("-"))]\n    if len(hits) == 1:\n        return hits[0], "contains"\n    if len(hits) > 1:\n        return None, f"ambiguous: {\', \'.join(hits)}"\n    return None, "no student folder"\n\n\ndef docx_text(path):\n    """Paragraph text of a .docx, one paragraph per line, no dependencies."""\n    with zipfile.ZipFile(path) as z:\n        xml = z.read("word/document.xml").decode("utf-8", "replace")\n    paras = re.split(r"</w:p>", "\\n".join(out)\n\n\ndef docx_words(path):\n    """Rough word count from a .docx without any third-party dependency."""\n    try:\n        with zipfile.ZipFile(path) as z:\n            xml = z.read("word/document.xml").decode("utf-8", "replace")\n    except Exception:\n        return None\n    text = re.sub(r"<[^>]+>", " ", xml)\n    return len(text.split())\n\n\ndef main():\n    args = os.path.join(TRANSCRIPTS, target)\n        sys.stdout.reconfigure(encoding="utf-8")\n        print(docx_text(target))\n        return 0\n    if not os.path.isdir(TRANSCRIPTS):\n        print(f"no    words=docx_words(p) if f.lower().endswith(".docx") else None,\n                         bytes=os.path.getsize(p)))\n\n    if "--json" in args:\n        print(json.dumps(rows, indent=2))\n        return 0\n\n    matched = [r for r in rows if r["student"] and not is_former(r["student"], dirs)]\n    former = [r for r in rows if r["student"] and is_former(r["student"], dirs)]\n    declared = [r [{'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Script completed\nWall time 5.5 seconds\nOutput:\n'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': '---\ntitle: Teaching Voice\ntype: concept\ntags: [lsat-u, voice, pedagogy, content]\ncreated: 2026-06-10\nupdated: 2026-07-18\nstatus: active\nsubject: Teaching Voice\naliases: []\n---\n\n# Teaching Voice\n\nHow LSAT U sounds, across every surface. This is the canonical voice doc: route all student-facing and brand copy through it. Built from a grill with Joshua (2026-06-13), then tested and enriched against the full corpus of his real correspondence (944 messages he authored, mid-2025 to mid-2026, from the Gmail takeout; 2026-07-18). Claims below marked with a quote are evidenced by that corpus.\n\nIt replaces the old two-register / 15-named-tools "preserve verbatim" profile (deleted 2026-06-10) and folds in the brand/marketing register the earlier draft was missing.\n\n## Core voice (every register)\n\nThe constant under all three registers below. This is Joshua on the page.\n\n- **Quiet authority.** State the value and let it land. Never oversell, never beg, never perform enthusiasm.\n- **Specific, never generic.** Real scores, the actual skill, the student\'s own history. Praise is a specific observation, not "great job."\n- **Honest about the work, gentle about the person.** Be blunt that the LSAT is hard ("expect this to be exhausting and very challenging"). Never be blunt about a student\'s shortcomings. Honesty points at the material; warmth points at the person. When someone slips, nudge gently, never accuse.\n- **Light, grounded metaphor, understated in email.** In his real correspondence the recurring image is quiet: "partner with you on your LSAT journey," "getting set up," "foundational." The vivid images (runway, climb, march toward November, an easy door to walk through) belong to authored teaching and brand copy, not to email. Keep metaphor light and grounded; never float off into abstraction.\n- **Balanced rhythm.** Short declaratives plus one slightly longer warm beat. Air between ideas. Each idea gets its own line. Real messages are short and single-purpose (median ~280 characters).\n- **Plain professional diction.** No corporate jargon, no startup hype ("unlock," "crush," "level up," "game-changer" — "crush" appears once in 944 messages). Contractions are the norm, not the exception. Exclamation points are genuine, not performed: a warm message often carries one, occasionally more, especially in openers ("Sorry for such a long delay!"). He is not exclamation-averse.\n- **Forward-looking.** End on the next step or what\'s ahead.\n- **No em dashes, ever.** Use periods, colons before lists, the middot (·) as a separator, and numbered steps for procedures.\n\n## Openings, closings, and signature phrases\n\nThe mechanical fingerprint of his email, from the real corpus. Match these when drafting as Joshua.\n\n- **Greeting.** "Hi [Name]," is the default (used ~519x). "Hey [Name]," for established/returning students (~229x, warmer). "Hello [Name]," (~105x) and "Dear [Name]," (~18x, formal) for first contact or a more formal note.\n- **Sign-off.** "Best," and "Best regards," are the workhorses (~360x / ~237x). "Thanks," when it\'s a favor or logistics (~146x). "Warmly," / "Warm regards," (~54x) for a genuinely warm note. "Talk soon," (~9x) for someone he\'ll see again soon.\n- **Signature.** Almost always signed **"Joshua"** (844 of 944 messages). The name is near-universal; include it.\n- **Signature phrases (his verbal fingerprint, use naturally, don\'t overuse):** "let me know" (by far the most common, ~390x), "looking forward," "I hope" / "hope all is well" / "hope you," "no worries at all," "happy to" / "more than happy to," "just wanted to make sure," "make sure," "no rush," "of course."\n- **Punctuation he actually uses:** semicolons (correctly, ~41x); ellipses essentially never. (For em-dashes, the hard rule in Core voice governs — never.)\n\n## The apology / accountability move\n\nOne of his most frequent and characteristic behaviors, and worth naming on its own. When he is late to reply, or missed or mishandled something, he opens by owning it plainly, often with a brief honest reason, then pivots straight to the fix. No over-apologizing, no excuses dressed up.\n\n> I\'m so sorry. I thought I had let you know ... I clearly didn\'t communicate that as well as I should have.\n\n> I\'ve been away from work for personal reasons, but I\'m back now and getting caught up.\n\nThe pattern: own it in the first line, give the real reason in one clause, move to what happens next. Warm, candid, brief.\n\n## When something on his side broke (approved shape, 2026-09-11)\n\nFrom the Sandra booking-error reply, edited by Joshua line by line over three drafts and then sent as-is. Use this shape whenever a student hit a bug or a mistake that was his. The sent text is the reference:\n\n> Hi Sandra,\n>\n> I\'m sorry about this. The error was on my end, not yours.\n>\n> To confirm: none of your bookings went through, so nothing is on the calendar yet. The page was showing a few times that the system then refused, and it looks like you landed on those. That is fixed now.\n>\n> Your link is the same one as before:\n> [link]\n>\n> Pick any time it shows and it will book. If it\'s easier, just send me the time you were trying for and I\'ll add it to the schedule myself.\n>\n> If you run into any other issues, let me know.\n>\n> Once again, my apologies.\n>\n> Best,\n> Joshua\n\n1. **Apology first, as the opening line.** "I\'m sorry about this. The error was on my end, not yours." The ownership sits in the first two sentences, before any explanation.\n2. **State their position plainly, as a confirmation.** "To confirm: none of your bookings went through, so nothing is on the calendar yet." Answer the question they actually asked. Don\'t mention the package or credits unless the situation calls for it.\n3. **One-sentence explanation, then "That is fixed now."** No mechanics, no system names.\n4. **Hand them the next step, plus the manual fallback.** The link, "pick any time it shows and it will book," and the offer to do it by hand: "If it\'s easier, just send me the time you were trying for and I\'ll add it to the schedule myself."\n5. **Invite the next report:** "If you run into any other issues, let me know."\n6. **Close with "Once again, my apologies."** then "Best," and "Joshua".\n\nCut from the draft, do not reuse:\n- "Sorry for the runaround" as a sign-off. The apology opens the email; it is not a closing quip.\n- "You will get a calendar invite with the Google Meet link right after." Do not narrate what the system will send; it reads as a promise about machinery.\n- "You have all 10 sessions" / "nothing was used from your package." Leave the package out unless it is needed; the reassurance they want is that nothing is booked, not an accounting.\n\n## Situational micro-templates\n\nVerbatim-grounded reference lines for the situations that recur most. Adapt, never paste blindly.\n\n- **Student reschedules / cancels:** low-pressure, no guilt.\n  > No worries at all. It happens, so please don\'t worry about it. If you would like to reschedule, just let me know.\n- **He missed / no-showed (approved make-good template):** full ownership, real reason, offer to make it right (see the apology move above). When the cause was an unexpected health issue, the approved shape is: sincerely apologize, state that a serious health scare unexpectedly took him out of commission, offer a **completely free, full LSAT session**, and hand them the complimentary booking link `https://cal.com/joshua-jtx5ud/complimentary-session`. Emphasis stays limited: bold the complimentary offer, italicize the line that one focused session can put points on the board. Draft in Gmail; never send without Joshua\'s explicit go-ahead.\n- **Consultation reminder (day-of):**\n  > Just checking in before our consultation today. Looking forward to speaking with you. I just wanted to make sure everything is still good.\n- **Consultation follow-up:** warm, specific to their situation.\n  > Really nice meeting you. I enjoyed our conversation ... I\'m glad we got to talk through where you\'re at and what you\'re aiming for on test day.\n- **Inbound prospect (hasn\'t booked):** state availability plainly, no overselling, hand them the next step.\n  > Thanks for reaching out ... I\'d be happy to talk more about what you\'re working on and see if we\'d be a good fit. You can schedule a consultation here.\n- **Student under real-life stress:** meet the person first.\n  > Please don\'t apologize ... it sounds like you are dealing with an incredibly stressful and demanding situation.\n\n## The three registers\n\nWhich voice governs which surface.\n\n### 1. Coaching (earnest) -- inbox, recaps, in-drill feedback, email\n\nFully earnest. Warm, sincere, calm, patient. No jokes. The closest thing to being in the room with Joshua. Normalizes struggle, then moves to the work.\n\nReference line (target tone):\n\n> Totally normal to trip on this one. Let\'s slow down: what is the author actually concluding? Once you see it, the trap answers lose their grip. You\'ve got this.\n\n- **Encouragement (student missed a hard one):** honest first, then forward. Name that it\'s genuinely hard, stay calm, move to the work. Not soft-reassuring, not cold.\n  > Missing this is expected. It\'s one of the hardest moves on the test. Let\'s slow down and see where it slipped.\n- **Accountability (student isn\'t doing the work):** gentle nudge, low pressure. Frame it as a slip, find a rhythm together. Never "the reps aren\'t happening," never tough love.\n- **Praise (student nails it):** name the exact skill, tie it to their history, raise the bar.\n  > That\'s the cleanest you\'ve split premise from conclusion yet. Let\'s push it into the harder sets.\n- **Hard truth about the test:** state it plainly. "Do not expect for it to come easy. Expect to find this exhausting."\n\n### 2. Teaching content (earnest substance, wit at the edges) -- bootcamp lessons, drill explanations\n\nThe substance stays earnest and clear (you are explaining a hard skill). The wit lives only at the edges: headers, openers, transitions. No jokes mid-explanation, nothing that costs comprehension.\n\n> Header: "The flaw hides in plain sight."\n> Body: earnest, clear, step by step.\n\n### 3. Brand (sharp wit) -- landing, auth, marketing\n\nConfident and clever, the way a good lawyer is clever. Wit tied to the real skill, not wordplay for its own sake. Playful is allowed, but every clever line must be earned and true. Hollow cleverness fails (the killed "the next card is the page in front of you" was clever but empty).\n\n> Most prep teaches the test. We teach the tell.\n\nBrand copy speaks as the platform ("we", "you"), not as an individual ("I", "Joshua"). The product is the coach; no single person narrates the marketing.\n\n## Don\'t\n\n- No cold-testing or gotcha tone. (Ties to teach-first-calibrate-after.)\n- No condescension or empty cheerleading. Encouragement must sit on real substance.\n- No generic praise, no hollow cleverness, no hedging ("you might want to").\n- No hype/startup vocabulary.\n- No em dashes, ever.\n\nCorrections log: [[COPY-CORRECTIONS]] records every student-facing wording fix and\nthe reason it was wrong. Read it before writing or editing LSAT U copy.\n\nRelated: teach-first-calibrate-after, LSAT U. Source samples: `raw/templates/Golden Email Template Playbook.md`, `raw/templates/email_writing_examples_11_full.txt`, and the full authored-email corpus from the Gmail takeout (944 messages, analyzed 2026-07-18; takeout at `raw/sources/private/takeout/`, git-ignored).\n\r\n# Copy corrections\n\nEvery student-facing wording fix, with the reason it was wrong. Read this before\nwriting or editing copy for LSAT U so the same mistake is not made twice.\n\nCompanion to [[teaching-voice]], which says how the writing should sound. This\nsays what has actually gone wrong and why.\n\nStarted 2026-09-07 from a Read, Recall, Colour pass. Add to it every time a\ncorrection is made.\n\n## The rules these corrections came from\n\nThree rules already existed and all three leaked anyway, because each was\nenforced on the components that happened to exist when it was written. A surface\nadded later starts uncovered.\n\n- **No em dashes, ever.** [[teaching-voice]], Core voice.\n- **No internal vocabulary in student copy.** `projects/lsatu/src/features/activity-centre/CONTEXT.md`\n  carries the glossary and marks what to avoid.\n- **Every CSS token a stylesheet uses must be defined in it.** `projects/lsatu/CLAUDE.md`.\n\nGuards now live with the content rather than with each component:\n`content/instructions-voice.test.ts` checks the authored instructions, so every\nsurface that renders them is covered, including surfaces not written yet.\n\n## Corrections\n\n### "Recall Rephrase Colour" → "Read, Recall, Colour"\nThe door\'s heading was hardcoded to a name the product does not have, one line\nunder a chip reading "Read, Recall, Colour". "Rephrase" belongs to a different\nActivity, Conditional Rephrase. A test asserted the wrong name, which is why\n2,600 passing tests never caught it.\n**Lesson:** when a test pins a string, check the string is right, not just that\nit matches.\n\n### "Intake only. Nothing comes back out yet…" → plain instruction\nClinical and abstract, and the sentence then told her to read "with full\nintonation" while step one is silent reading. The clause that made intonation\ninternal, "hear it naturally in your head", had been dropped in an earlier edit.\n**Lesson:** a word like "intake" reads as jargon. And when copy is trimmed,\ncheck what the trimmed clause was load-bearing for.\n\n### "Three beats through the stimulus" → "Three steps"\n"Beat" is the internal code name for one of the four method steps. The glossary\nsays students see **step**. The interface ten pixels below labelled the same four\nthings Step 1 to Step 4, so the page used two names for one thing.\n**Lesson:** never let an implementation name reach the page.\n\n### "22 pieces to read" → line removed\nA **piece** is one chunk, roughly a sentence, and the instructions on that same\npage use the word that way. The count was of stimuli, so "22 pieces" read as 22\nsentences.\n**Lesson:** a unit word must mean one thing per surface. Check what a word\nalready means on the page before reusing it.\n\n### "say it back" → "tell it back", "The Read" → "The Recall"\nThe library door still carried both retired names. "The Read" was step four\'s\nformer name and collided with step one, which is why it was renamed.\n**Lesson:** a rename is not finished until every row carries it. The door was\nstale for months because it is a different database row from the sections.\n\n### "then a fourth" → "then a fourth step"\nThe noun sat three words back and the reader had to carry it.\n\n### "once you have got all of it" → "once you have read all of it"\nAmbiguous between having read it and having remembered it, in the one clause\nthat triggers step four.\n**Lesson:** precision matters most where the sentence is an instruction.\n\n### The three-fact notice → one fact\n"Nothing is recording yet, the microphone opens on Start, and the section\nrecords in one take that you cannot pause." Two of those are said again in step\nfour and in the long version, so she skipped the paragraph.\n**Lesson:** say it once, in the place it matters.\n\n### The method, told twice → the long version collapsed\nThe page rendered four numbered steps and then the whole written briefing saying\nthe same thing at length, both open. She read the method twice and could not\ntell which one to follow.\n**Lesson:** two explanations of one thing is worse than either alone.\n\n### "PT105.S1 · 24 stimuli · about 25 min" → removed\nThe section was already the second line of the title. The clock is at the foot\nand in the long version. The stimulus count measured the work in a unit she has\nno feel for.\n**Lesson:** delete a line that repeats what is above it. Do not reword it.\n\n## Booking emails: hand over the link, not the pass settings (2026-09-08)\n\n**Cut:** "70 minutes each, and no expiration date, so there\'s no rush to use them."\n**Keep:** "You\'re set up on LSAT U with 10 sessions."\n\nSession length and expiry are admin fields. The student sees them on the booking\npage when she picks a time, so putting them in the email is detail she did not ask\nfor and has to read past to reach the link. The credit count is worth saying because\nit tells her how much she has. Everything else about the pass stays in the backend.\n\n**Lesson:** in a booking email, say who it\'s for, how many sessions, and the link.\nStop there.\n\n## Drill hub: say what the button does, not what the feature is called (2026-09-09)\n\nSix changes on `/classroom/drill`, from the run-3 pass. The hub named its own\nfeatures, and it assumed the student had rejected something.\n\n| Was | Now |\n|---|---|\n| "Start Smart Drill" | "Practice your weakest types" |\n| "Start One Passage" | "Read one passage" |\n| "Start a Smart Drill instead" | "Or practice your weakest types" |\n| "Read one passage instead" | "Or read one passage now" |\n| "Open analytics" | "See where you lose points" |\n| "Open journal" | "Review your missed questions" |\n\n"Smart Drill" is the product\'s internal name for the adaptive set. On a button it\nasks the student to guess what she is about to get. The sentence above the button\nstill names it, which is where a product name belongs: after the thing has been\nexplained, not as the explanation.\n\n"Instead" was the worse one. It tells the student she has just declined the\nassigned work by reading past it. She has not. "Or" offers a second path without\nnarrating a decision she never made.\n\n"Open analytics" and "Open journal" name a screen. A student does not want\nanalytics, she wants to know where the points are going.\n\nThe fallback paragraph lost "an adaptive set that follows your weakest question\ntypes" for "the question types you miss most": the same fact, without the product\nvocabulary.\n\n**Lesson:** a button says what happens next, in the student\'s words. Feature names\nbelong in the sentence that explains them, never on the control.\n\n## Words never to use in student copy\n\nFrom the glossary. Internal names may stay in code, never on the page.\n\n| Never | Use instead |\n|---|---|\n| beat, beats | step |\n| chunk | piece |\n| intake | plain instruction |\n| briefing, phase, tab, card | the thing\'s own name |\n| say it back | tell it back |\n| The Read | The Recall |\n| Recall Rephrase Colour | Read, Recall, Colour |\n| em dash, en dash | a full stop, or a colon before a list |\n\nRelated: [[teaching-voice]] · [[ASSIGN-AN-ACTIVITY]] · [[STUDENT-PLATFORM-IDENTITY-MAP]]\n\r\n---\ntitle: Sofia Transcripts\ntype: person\ntags: [lsat-u, student, transcript, sofia]\ncreated: Line 1137, position 26.\r\n---\ntitle: Recap · Sofia · 2026-09-09\ntype: recap\nrecord_kind: primary\nstudent: sofia\nsession_date: 2026-09-09\nsource: transcript-downloads/2026-09-09-sofia-notes-by-gemini.md\nstatus: draft\nposted: false\nposted_at:\n---\n\n# Session recap · 2026-09-09\n\nHey Sofia,\n\nTwo parallel questions today, one causal and one conditional, and a new way to write your wrong answer journal. You had the right instincts on both questions. The work now is turning instinct into a check you run before you look at the answers.\n\n## What we worked on\n\n- SMACKER: the five places a question can beat you. Structure, Method of reasoning, Assumption, Keywords, Ranking the choices. Every miss is one of these five.\n- Wrong answer journal, upgraded. "I didn\'t understand it" is true but useless. Which of the five went wrong? That is the entry.\n- The principal question (causal parallel). The argument is a causal claim, then a correlation, then a fact about what the principal concluded. The right answer needs all three, in that order.\n- The societal values question (conditional parallel). The stimulus denies the sufficient condition and concludes the necessary condition fails. False contrapositive.\n- Keywords that actually matter: "must", "invariably", and the pivot "but". Premise indicators like "since" tell you nothing, because every argument has a premise.\n\n## The one thing to hold onto\n\nFind the flaw before you touch the answer choices.\n\nOn the principal question, the flaw was a root cause assumed fixed just because the symptom disappeared. Once you name that, A falls apart on its own: A runs the timeline backwards (they stopped overeating, then the weight gain stopped). D runs it the right way (the complaints stopped, then the manager assumed the workers were busy). You could not see that difference until you had the flaw in hand.\n\nOn the societal values question, the flaw was sufficient versus necessary. Once you named it, B was dead before you read it to the end: "usually" does not match "invariably", and there is no pivot.\n\nName the crime, then go find the answer that commits the same crime. Half of parallel flaw questions are a classic: sufficient versus necessary, or correlation read as cause.\n\n## Where it slipped\n\nYou held onto "since" and "must" and nearly picked B over D. Normal. Premise indicators feel important because they are easy to spot. They are not a standout feature. A pivot is, because not every argument has one. When you see "but", "yet", or "however" in the stimulus, the right answer almost has to carry one too.\n\nThe other slip was strength. "Invariably" means every time. An answer that says "usually" is off before you check anything else. Match the strength first; it is the fastest elimination you have.\n\n## Before next session\n\n- [ ] Rewrite your recent wrong answer journal entries using SMACKER. For each miss, name the one component that failed.\n- [ ] The Parallel Flaw + Famous Flaws drill I assigned, and the Parallel Reasoning note in your Classroom. Read the note first. Before each question, write the flaw in one line, then go to the choices.\n\n## Next time\n\nMore parallel work, and we will check whether the flaw-first habit is holding under time.\n\nBest,\nJoshua\n\n---\n\n## Notes for me (not posted)\n\n- **Weak spots:** premise indicators mistaken for standout features; strength matching not yet reflexive; goes to the choices before naming the flaw (she said so herself at 00:38).\n- **Follow-ups on my side:** parallel drill + note assigned 2026-09-11 (see assignment-log.md).\n- **Watch:** her instincts on the correct answer were good both times (D on both questions) before she could explain why. The gap is articulation, not intuition. These skills infer from context first and ask only short blocking questions when needed.\r\n\r\n## Output & Organization\r\n\r\nUnless the user specifies to return in context, write results to `.firecrawl/` with `-o`. Add `.firecrawl/` to `.gitignore`. Always quote URLs - shell interprets `?` and `&` as special characters.\r\n\r\n```bash\r\nfirecrawl search "react hooks" -o .firecrawl/search-react-hooks.json --json\r\nfirecrawl scrape "<url>" -o .firecrawl/page.md\r\n```\r\n\r\nNaming conventions:\r\n\r\n```\r\n.firecrawl/search-{query}.json\r\n.firecrawl/search-{query}-scraped.json\r\n.firecrawl/{site}-{path}.md\r\n```\r\n\r\nRead output files incrementally with `grep`, `head`, or bounded reads:\r\n\r\n```bash\r\nwc -l .firecrawl/file.md && head -50 .firecrawl/file.md\r\ngrep -n "keyword" .firecrawl/file.md\r\n```\r\n\r\nSingle format outputs raw content. Multiple formats (e.g., `--format markdown,links`) output JSON. Use `jq` to work with JSON output, e.g. `jq -r \'.data.web[].url\' .firecrawl/search.json`.\r\n\r\n## Feedback\r\n\r\nAfter using search results, send `firecrawl search-feedback` (the first feedback per search refunds 1 credit). The full pattern, guard, and rules live in [firecrawl-search](../firecrawl-search/SKILL.md).\r\n\r\nFor non-search endpoint jobs, use `firecrawl feedback <endpoint> <jobId>` to send concise job-level feedback through `/v2/feedback`. Supported endpoints are `search`, `scrape`, `parse`, and `map`.\r\n\r\n```bash\r\nfirecrawl feedback scrape "$SCRAPE_ID" \\\r\n  --rating partial \\\r\n  --issues missing_markdown \\\r\n  --tags docs \\\r\n  --note "The pricing table was missing from the markdown output." \\\r\n  --url "https://example.com/pricing" \\\r\n  --page-numbers 1 \\\r\n  --silent &\r\n```\r\n\r\nKeep generic feedback small: issue codes, tags, short notes, URLs, page numbers, and small metadata objects — never raw scrape/parse outputs or full page contents.\r\n\r\n**Opt out:** `export FIRECRAWL_NO_ENDPOINT_FEEDBACK=1` makes the CLI skip every endpoint feedback call silently. Respect that flag — do not try to work around it.\r\n\r\n## Parallelization\r\n\r\nRun independent operations in parallel. Check `firecrawl --status` for concurrency limit:\r\n\r\n```bash\r\nfirecrawl scrape "<url-1>" -o .firecrawl/1.md &\r\nfirecrawl scrape "<url-2>" -o .firecrawl/2.md &\r\nfirecrawl scrape "<url-3>" -o .firecrawl/3.md &\r\nwait\r\n```\r\n\r\nFor interact, scrape multiple pages and interact with each independently using their scrape IDs.\r\n\r\n## Credit Usage\r\n\r\n```bash\r\nfirecrawl credit-usage\r\nfirecrawl credit-usage --json --pretty -o .firecrawl/credits.json\r\n```\r\n\r\n---\r\nname: firecrawl-search\r\ndescription: |\r\n  Web search with full page content. Use when no URL is known: finding sources, articles, or news. For papers use firecrawl-research-index; for library, API, error, or bug questions use firecrawl-developer-index.\r\nallowed-tools:\r\n  - Bash(firecrawl *)\r\n  - Bash(npx firecrawl-cli *)\r\n---\r\n\r\n# firecrawl search\r\n\r\nWeb search with optional content scraping. Returns search results as JSON, optionally with full page content.\r\n\r\n## Quick start\r\n\r\n```bash\r\n# Basic search\r\nfirecrawl search "your query" -o .firecrawl/result.json --json\r\n\r\n# Search and scrape full page content from results\r\nfirecrawl search "your query" --scrape -o .firecrawl/scraped.json --json\r\n\r\n# News from the past day\r\nfirecrawl search "your query" --sources news --tbs qdr:d -o .firecrawl/news.json --json\r\n```\r\n\r\nRun `firecrawl search --help` for the full option list.\r\n\r\n`--categories developer` weighs the developer index beside ordinary web results in this same call (no passage control, no index filters). `--categories research` is a website filter, not the paper index. Dedicated skills: [firecrawl-developer-index](../firecrawl-developer-index/SKILL.md) and [firecrawl-research-index](../firecrawl-research-index/SKILL.md).\r\n\r\n**Done when:** results are saved under `.firecrawl/`, verified non-empty, processed for the request, and one feedback event is sent within the time window (unless opted out).\r\n\r\n## Tips\r\n\r\n- **`--highlights` on by default:** results are query-relevant excerpts, not full-page snippets. Use `--no-highlights` for the original snippets.\r\n- **`--scrape` fetches full content** — reuse that content instead of re-scraping result URLs. This saves credits and avoids redundant fetches.\r\n- Always write results to `.firecrawl/` with `-o` to avoid context window bloat.\r\n- Use `jq` to extract URLs or titles: `jq -r \'.data.web[].url\' .firecrawl/search.json`\r\n- Naming convention: `.firecrawl/search-{query}.json` or `.firecrawl/search-{query}-scraped.json`\r\n\r\n## Send feedback after every search (refunds 1 credit)\r\n\r\nSearch costs 2 credits. After you\'ve actually used the results (or decided they were useless), send structured feedback with `firecrawl search-feedback <id>`. The first feedback per search refunds 1 credit and helps us improve search quality. **Do this once per search**, in the background, after you finish processing the results — it does not block your main task.\r\n\r\n**Opt out:** if `FIRECRAWL_NO_SEARCH_FEEDBACK=1` (or `FIRECRAWL_DISABLE_SEARCH_FEEDBACK=1`) is set, the CLI silently skips the call and never sends anything. Respect that — do not try to work around it. (Team admins can also disable this server-side; the API will return `feedbackErrorCode: "TEAM_OPTED_OUT"` and the CLI will exit 0 silently.)\r\n\r\n**Rules to know before you call this:**\r\n\r\n- **Time window:** must be sent within ~2 minutes of the search. Late feedback is rejected.\r\n- **`--missing-content` is the most important field.** It\'s a list of _specific pieces_ of content you expected but did not find. One topic per entry, each in its own string. These aggregate across teams and tell us what to index next.\r\n- **Substantive content required** (zero-effort feedback is rejected with HTTP 400):\r\n  - `good` → must include at least one `--valuable-sources` entry.\r\n  - `partial` → must include `--valuable-sources` or `--missing-content`.\r\n  - `bad` → must include `--missing-content` or `--query-suggestions`.\r\n- **Daily refund cap (per team, per UTC day, default 100 credits).** Once your team has been refunded 100 credits today, further submissions still record feedback but no longer refund credits. The response includes `creditsRefundedToday` / `dailyRefundCap` / `dailyCapReached`. **When `dailyCapReached: true`, stop calling `search-feedback` for the rest of the UTC day** — it won\'t refund anything and you\'re wasting bandwidth.\r\n- **Idempotent:** re-submitting for the same search id returns success but no extra refund.\r\n- **`--silent &`** is the right pattern — exit code 0 even on failure, so a rejected/expired call never crashes your pipeline.\r\n\r\nVerify the search returned results before reading its `id`. Zero-result searches write no output file, so the file may be missing — or left over from an earlier search. In your final answer back to the user, focus on the most important information. Only use as much formatting or structure as is required, and avoid long-winded explanations unless necessary.

### Formatting rules

Your answer is being rendered by an application for the user. Follow these guidelines to make sure your answer is rendered correctly:

- You may format with GitHub-flavored Markdown.

  * Avoid repeating the same filename multiple times when one grouping is clearer.

### Visualizations

Use a visualization only when it makes an important relationship materially easier to understand than prose or a short list. Do not add one merely because an answer has components or steps.

Good candidates include:

- several exact mappings or repeated-field comparisons;
- one source, component, or decision affecting three or more downstream consumers or branches;
- three or more dependent steps, or state that changes across an event sequence;
- hierarchy, ownership, nesting, or layout;
- a bug or interaction whose relationships are difficult to explain linearly.

Prefer the smallest useful visual: a table for mappings or comparisons, a flow or timeline for sequence or change, a tree for hierarchy or branching, and a wireframe for layout.

Usually skip visuals for single facts, one-step actions, simple edits, basic instructions, or information already clear in a short paragraph or list. Compact notation and small examples do not count as visualizations.

# Rules for getting work done

- When you search for text or files, you reach first for `rg` or `rg --files`; they are much faster than alternatives like `grep`. If `rg` is unavailable, you use the next best tool without fuss.
- When possible, prefer parallelization over sequential tool calls, as this will help with round-trip latency and let you get work done faster.
- Do not chain shell commands with separators like `echo "====";` or `printf '---'`; the output becomes noisy in a way that makes the user's side of the conversation worse.

## File editing constraints

Use `apply_patch` for local file edits. Do not create or edit files with `cat` or other shell write tricks. Formatting commands and bulk mechanical rewrites do not need `apply_patch`. Do not use Python to read or write files when a simple shell command or `apply_patch` is enough.

- Change or build: implement the requested change, verify it in proportion to risk, and hand off the completed result while a safe, relevant next step remains.
- Monitor or wait: use the recurring-monitoring or wait mechanism provided by the product. Unchanged external state is expected and is not by itself a blocker.

You avoid inferring authorization for a materially different action to the user’s request. Bias towards taking action in the following circumstances:

That skill defines the fundamental RED-GREEN-REFACTOR cycle. This skill adapts TDD to documentation.\r\n\r\n**Official guidance:** For Anthropic\'s official skill authoring best practices, see anthropic-best-practices.md. This document provides additional patterns and guidelines that complement the TDD-focused approach in this skill.\r\n\r\n## What is a Skill?\r\n\r\nA **skill** is a reference guide for proven techniques, patterns, or tools. Skills help future Claude instances find and apply effective approaches.\r\n\r\n**Skills are:** Reusable techniques, patterns, tools, reference guides\r\n\r\n**Skills are NOT:** Narratives about how you solved a problem once\r\n\r\n## TDD Mapping for Skills\r\n\r\n| TDD Concept | Skill Creation |\r\n|-------------|----------------|\r\n| **Test case** | Pressure scenario with subagent |\r\n| **Production code** | Skill document (SKILL.md) |\r\n| **Test fails (RED)** | Agent violates rule without skill (baseline) |\r\n| **Test passes (GREEN)** | Agent complies with skill present |\r\n| **Refactor** | Close loopholes while maintaining compliance |\r\n| **Write test first** | Run baseline scenario BEFORE writing skill |\r\n| **Watch it fail** | Document exact rationalizations agent uses |\r\n| **Minimal code** | Write skill addressing those specific violations |\r\n| **Watch it pass** | Verify agent now complies |\r\n| **Refactor cycle** | Find new rationalizations → plug → re-verify |\r\n\r\nThe entire skill creation process follows RED-GREEN-REFACTOR.\r\n\r\n## When to Create a Skill\r\n\r\n**Create when:**\r\n- Technique wasn\'t intuitively obvious to you\r\n- You\'d reference this again across projects\r\n- Pattern applies broadly (not project-specific)\r\n- Others would benefit\r\n\r\n**Don\'t create for:**\r\n- One-off solutions\r\n- Standard practices well-documented elsewhere\r\n- Project-specific conventions (put in CLAUDE.md)\r\n- Mechanical constraints (if it\'s enforceable with regex/validation, automate it—save documentation for judgment calls)\r\n\r\n## Skill Types\r\n\r\n### Technique\r\nConcrete method with steps to follow (condition-based-waiting, root-cause-tracing)\r\n\r\n### Pattern\r\nWay of thinking about problems (flatten-with-flags, test-invariants)\r\n\r\n### Reference\r\nAPI docs, syntax guides, tool documentation (office docs)\r\n\r\n## Directory Structure\r\n\r\n\r\n```\r\nskills/\r\n  skill-name/\r\n    SKILL.md              # Main reference (required)\r\n    supporting-file.*     # Only if needed\r\n```\r\n\r\n**Flat namespace** - all skills in one searchable namespace\r\n\r\n**Separate files for:**\r\n1. **Heavy reference** (100+ lines) - API docs, comprehensive syntax\r\n2. **Reusable tools** - Scripts, utilities, templates\r\n\r\n**Keep inline:**\r\n- Principles and concepts\r\n- Code patterns (< 50 lines)\r\n- Everything else\r\n\r\n## SKILL.md Structure\r\n\r\n**Frontmatter (YAML):**\r\n- Two required fields: `name` and `description` (see [agentskills.io/specification](https://agentskills.io/specification) for all supported fields)\r\n- Max 1024 characters total\r\n- `name`: Use letters, numbers, and hyphens only (no parentheses, special chars)\r\n- `description`: Third-person, describes ONLY when to use (NOT what it does)\r\n  - Start with "Use when..." to focus on triggering conditions\r\n  - Include specific symptoms, situations, and contexts\r\n  - **NEVER summarize the skill\'s process or workflow** (see CSO section for why)\r\n  - Keep under 500 characters if possible\r\n\r\n```markdown\r\n---\r\nname: Skill-Name-With-Hyphens\r\ndescription: Use when [specific triggering conditions and symptoms]\r\n---\r\n\r\n# Skill Name\r\n\r\n## Overview\r\nWhat is this? Core principle in 1-2 sentences.\r\n\r\n## When to Use\r\n[Small inline flowchart IF decision non-obvious]\r\n\r\nBullet list with SYMPTOMS and use cases\r\nWhen NOT to use\r\n\r\n## Core Pattern (for techniques/patterns)\r\nBefore/after code comparison\r\n\r\n## Quick Reference\r\nTable or bullets for scanning common operations\r\n\r\n## Implementation\r\nInline code for simple patterns\r\nLink to file for heavy reference or reusable tools\r\n\r\n## Common Mistakes\r\nWhat goes wrong + fixes\r\n\r\n## Real-World Impact (optional)\r\nConcrete results\r\n```\r\n\r\n\r\n## Claude Search Optimization (CSO)\r\n\r\n**Critical for discovery:** Future Claude needs to FIND your skill\r\n\r\n### 1. Rich Description Field\r\n\r\n**Purpose:** Claude reads description to decide which skills to load for a given task. Make it answer: "Should I read this skill right now?"\r\n\r\n**Format:** Start with "Use when..." to focus on triggering conditions\r\n\r\n**CRITICAL: Description = When to Use, NOT What the Skill Does**\r\n\r\nThe description should ONLY describe triggering conditions. Do NOT summarize the skill\'s process or workflow in the description.\r\n\r\n**Why this matters:** Testing revealed that when a description summarizes the skill\'s workflow, Claude may follow the description instead of reading the full skill content. A description saying "code review between tasks" caused Claude to do ONE review, even though the skill\'s flowchart clearly showed TWO reviews (spec compliance then code quality).\r\n\r\nWhen the description was changed to just "Use when executing implementation plans with independent tasks" (no workflow summary), Claude correctly read the flowchart and followed the two-stage review process.\r\n\r\n**The trap:** Descriptions that summarize workflow create a shortcut Claude will take. The skill body becomes documentation Claude skips.\r\n\r\n```yaml\r\n# ❌ BAD: Summarizes workflow - Claude may follow this instead of reading skill\r\ndescription: Use when executing plans - dispatches subagent per task with code review between tasks\r\n\r\n# ❌ BAD: Too much process detail\r\ndescription: Use for TDD - write test first, watch it fail, write minimal code, refactor\r\n\r\n# ✅ GOOD: Just triggering conditions, no workflow summary\r\ndescription: Use when executing implementation plans with independent tasks in the current session\r\n\r\n# ✅ GOOD: Triggering conditions only\r\ndescription: Use when implementing any feature or bugfix, before writing implementation code\r\n```\r\n\r\n**Content:**\r\n- Use concrete triggers, symptoms, and situations that signal this skill applies\r\n- Describe the *problem* (race conditions, inconsistent behavior) not *language-specific symptoms* (setTimeout, sleep)\r\n- Keep triggers technology-agnostic unless the skill itself is technology-specific\r\n- If skill is technology-specific, make that explicit in the trigger\r\n- Write in third person (injected into system prompt)\r\n- **NEVER summarize the skill\'s process or workflow**\r\n\r\n```yaml\r\n# ❌ BAD: Too abstract, vague, doesn\'t include when to use\r\ndescription: For async testing\r\n\r\n# ❌ BAD: First person\r\ndescription: I can help you with async tests when they\'re flaky\r\n\r\n# ❌ BAD: Mentions technology but skill isn\'t specific to it\r\ndescription: Use when tests use setTimeout/sleep and are flaky\r\n\r\n# ✅ GOOD: Starts with "Use when", describes problem, no workflow\r\ndescription: Use when tests have race conditions, timing dependencies, or pass/fail inconsistently\r\n\r\n# ✅ GOOD: Technology-specific skill with explicit trigger\r\ndescription: Use when using React Router and handling authentication redirects\r\n```\r\n\r\n### 2. Keyword Coverage\r\n\r\nUse words Claude would search for:\r\n- Error messages: "Hook timed out", "ENOTEMPTY", "race condition"\r\n- Symptoms: "flaky", "hanging", "zombie", "pollution"\r\n- Synonyms: "timeout/hang/freeze", "cleanup/teardown/afterEach"\r\n- Tools: Actual commands, library names, file types\r\n\r\n### 3. Descriptive Naming\r\n\r\n**Use active voice, verb-first:**\r\n- ✅ `creating-skills` not `skill-creation`\r\n- ✅ `condition-based-waiting` not `async-test-helpers`\r\n\r\n### 4. Token Efficiency (Critical)\r\n\r\n**Problem:** getting-started and frequently-referenced skills load into EVERY conversation. Every token counts.\r\n\r\n**Target word counts:**\r\n- getting-started workflows: <150 words each\r\n- Frequently-loaded skills: <200 words total\r\n- Other skills: <500 words (still be concise)\r\n\r\n**Techniques:**\r\n\r\n**Move details to tool help:**\r\n```bash\r\n# ❌ BAD: Document all flags in SKILL.md\r\nsearch-conversations supports --text, --both, --after DATE, --before DATE, --limit N\r\n\r\n# ✅ GOOD: Reference --help\r\nsearch-conversations supports multiple modes and filters. Run --help for details.\r\n```\r\n\r\n**Use cross-references:**\r\n```markdown\r\n# ❌ BAD: Repeat workflow details\r\nWhen searching, dispatch subagent with template...\r\n[20 lines of repeated instructions]\r\n\r\n# ✅ GOOD: Reference other skill\r\nAlways use subagents (50-100x context savings). The standards-committee explanation is especially useful because it explicitly notes that a stimulus can contain no facts.\n+\n+## Ranked research for a reusable post-session-note skill\n+\n+The Firecrawl agent scored each candidate from 1 to 5. Use retrieval practice as the learning loop, worked examples and cognitive-load principles for explanations, backward design for next steps, and UNC's audience/plain-language rules for the prose. Use the Anthropic repository only as a packaging reference.\n+\n+The proposed note shape is:\n+\n+1. **Main takeaway:** one transferable LSAT concept or decision rule.\n+2. **How to use it:** cue, reasoning move, and common trap.\n+3. **What the work showed:** evidence-based diagnostic, with fact separated from interpretation.\n+4. **Practice next:** one retrieval prompt and one concrete transfer task with a success criterion.\n+5. **Watch-for:** only if the session left a real uncertainty.\n+\n+The skill should explicitly forbid chronological play-by-play, praise for merely choosing a correct answer, answer-key dumping, unsupported claims about improvement, generic motivational filler, and invented student beliefs. It should require a scan test: the student can find the main concept and next action in under two minutes.\n+\n+### Backups\n+\n+- **Cognitive Load Theory in Practice** is the best backup when the difficulty is explaining a complex LSAT reasoning process without overwhelming the student. Keep the worked example short and fade the scaffold.\n+- **UNC Business Writing** is the best backup when the difficulty is tone, organization, or concision. It cannot replace a learning-science diagnostic.\n+\n+## Source-backed principles to carry into the skill\n+\n+- Retrieval is a learning strategy, not only an assessment. [Retrieval Practice Guide](https://pdf.retrievalpractice.org/RetrievalPracticeGuide.pdf), “What is retrieval practice?”\n+- Worked examples should make every important reasoning step visible, then guidance should fade. [Cognitive Load Theory in Practice](https://education.nsw.gov.au/content/dam/main-education/about-us/educational-data/cese/2017-cognitive-load-theory-practice-guide.pdf), “Strategy 2: Use worked examples.”\n+- Start with the capability the student should demonstrate, then choose evidence and practice that match it. [UIC Backward Design](https://teaching.uic.edu/cate-teaching-guides/syllabus-course-design/backward-design/).\n+- Write for the actual reader. The student is capable but does not share the tutor's context, so the note must define the needed term and carry the reasoning. [UNC Audience](https://writingcenter.unc.edu/tips-and-tools/audience/).\n+\n+## Caveats\n+\n+This is a research synthesis and design proposal, not proof that one public source already contains the exact skill we need. The retrieval guide and NSW PDF had no clearly established reuse license in the fetched material. UNC and CMU pages state Creative Commons terms; adapt principles rather than copying their prose. Anthropic's repository has mixed licensing by subdirectory. Human review remains necessary for LSAT logic, student diagnosis, privacy, and any claim about progress.\n*** End Patch";
text(await tools.apply_patch(patch));

The credit count is worth saying because\r\nit tells her how much she has. "Or" offers a second path without\r\nnarrating a decision she never made.\r\n\r\n"Open analytics" and "Open journal" name a screen. That keeps the stimulus manageable and prevents an answer choice from quietly changing the logic.\r\n\r\n## Separate facts from rules\r\n\r\nA **fact** is something the stimulus gives you as true about a case or situation.\r\n\r\nA **rule** is a general conditional: if its trigger is present, its result must follow. A rule does not tell you that the trigger actually occurred.\r\n\r\nThat distinction matters because some Must Be True stimuli contain rules but no facts. The contract-negotiator set was an example. The statements supplied several general relationships, but no separate case that triggered one of them. The job there was to chain the rules.\r\n\r\nWhen a fact is supplied, ask whether it matches a rule's trigger. If the direct trigger is absent, check whether a known result is false so that you can use the contrapositive.\r\n\r\n## Find the bridge\r\n\r\nWhen there are multiple rules, look for the idea that appears in the necessary position of one rule and the sufficient position of another. That repeated idea is the bridge.\r\n\r\n```text\r\nA → B\r\nB → C\r\n\r\nTherefore: A → C\r\n```\r\n\r\nThe useful inference is usually between the two loose ends, A and C. The repeated idea, B, is there to connect them. Do not chain two statements merely because they share a word; the word has to sit in the position needed for the link.\r\n\r\n## Keep the arrow honest\r\n\r\nWrite the trigger first and the guaranteed result second. Then test the answer against that exact direction.\r\n\r\n```text\r\nBurning a large amount of trash in an incinerator → wasting resources\r\n\r\nValid contrapositive:\r\nnot wasting resources → do not burn a large amount of trash in an incinerator\r\n\r\nInvalid reversal:\r\nwasting resources → burning a large amount of trash in an incinerator\r\n```\r\n\r\nThe first line is the conditional relationship. The second is its contrapositive: reverse the direction and negate both sides. The third is the invalid reversal. Wasting resources does not prove that this particular incinerator practice caused it.\r\n\r\nWhen your reading and your diagram seem to disagree, return to the sentence that created the arrow. Ask two questions:\r\n\r\n1. What is the trigger?\r\n2. What result does the sentence guarantee?\r\n\r\nThat check is more reliable than rebuilding the whole stimulus from memory. Keep each statement in the role the stimulus gives it. Do not invent a fact to trigger a rule, and do not turn a general rule into a claim that its trigger occurred.\r\n\r\n## Before next session\r\n\r\n- [ ] Complete the conditional-diagramming practice I assign.
